brief: We sell protein bars that don't taste like cardboard. That's basically the whole pitch.

profile.brief: We sell protein bars that don't taste like cardboard. That's basically the whole pitch.
profile.business_summary: A protein bar brand whose pitch is that the bars actually taste good.

price_tier.note: No pricing given; mid is typical for protein bar brands

first_order_value_usd.note: Typical multi-box or variety-pack first order for snack bars

age_range.note: Typical buyers of better-tasting protein snacks

audience.value: Adults who eat protein bars for workouts or on-the-go snacking and dislike how most bars taste

picks.name: The Fitness Enthusiast
picks.why_plausible: The brief targets adults who eat protein bars for workouts, and this persona works out 4+ times weekly with affinities in supplements and recovery and low-medium price sensitivity. Protein bars are a core replenishment buy for them.
lean_into: performance claims (protein per bar, post-workout fuel)
fuel that actually performs and tastes good
identity as part of a training routine
avoid: athlete endorsements the brand can't truthfully claim
picks.ad_angle: Post-workout protein you'll actually look forward to eating — real macros, no chalky aftertaste.

picks.name: The Wellness Optimizer
picks.why_plausible: She buys supplements, wellness and organic grocery, and pays premiums (price_sensitivity: low, AOV $95), so a protein bar is a routine category. Her one risk is 'ultra-processed food', so the ad must lead with what's in the bar, not just the flavor gimmick.
lean_into: outcome-focused: protein grams that fit her macros
taste without compromising on what's in it
avoid: science-y claims the brief can't back
anything that reads as candy-bar junk food
picks.ad_angle: A bar that meets her ingredient standards and still tastes like something she wants to eat — no trade-off between clean and edible.

picks.name: The Convenience-First Millennial
picks.why_plausible: Urban, convenience-driven snacker (affinities: quick_commerce, subscription_services) whose default is whatever's easy — a grab-and-go bar is exactly that, and $35 sits under their $55 typical AOV. Scored mid because tags miss that 'on-the-go snacking' is literally the brief's stated audience.
picks.ad_angle: The desk-drawer/gym-bag default: a fast meal-gap fix that doesn't taste like a punishment.

picks.name: The Gen Z Aesthete
picks.why_plausible: The brand's values skew playful (1.0) and her messaging preferences are playful, novelty and brand voice — the 'doesn't taste like cardboard' line is written for her. She already buys functional beverages and small-batch snack brands at a $48 AOV.
avoid: dry performance-spec claims with no personality
picks.ad_angle: Lead with the joke: most protein bars taste like cardboard, ours doesn't — flavor-forward and unserious.

picks.name: The Busy Parent
picks.why_plausible: Time-poor dual-income parent who buys convenience snacks in bulk for the household; a bar the whole family will actually eat solves the 'bought it, nobody touched it' problem. Ranked low only because the tags read protein bars as fitness, not as a pantry staple.
lean_into: time-saving grab-and-go for school and practice runs
picks.ad_angle: The lunchbox and glovebox staple that doesn't get left uneaten — bulk-friendly snacking the whole house agrees on.

plan.summary: Budget leans to the three publishers where the checkout itself is a fitness or better-for-you-food moment (Studiogrid classes, Movewell activewear, Pop & Sip functional drinks), with tests on supplement, pantry, convenience-delivery and activewear-footwear baskets to see whether replenishment and impulse snacking convert; pet, beauty, home and older-skewing apparel are excluded as unconnected purchase moments.

recommended.name: Studiogrid
recommended.tier_reason: The score treated this as a loose wellness adjacency, but the purchase moment is literally a booked workout: notes say users are 'actively spending on self-care and fitness', so a post-workout protein bar is the natural next buy, and $35 sits under the $42 typical basket.
recommended.rationale: Someone who just booked a fitness class or personal training session is the core protein-bar buyer; 13.6M impressions of high-income, actively-training shoppers at a $42 basket makes the $35 offer an easy add.

evidence.quote: Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

recommended.risk: Spa and yoga bookings dilute the hard-training segment, and a 74% female skew may index toward lighter-nutrition products than a protein bar.

recommended.name: Movewell
recommended.tier_reason: Scored as a generic category adjacency, but the notes state these are 'Fitness-engaged shoppers' buying activewear — the workout-gear purchase moment leads directly to workout fuel, and at 22M impressions with a $78 basket the $35 bar is a cheap add-on.
recommended.rationale: Activewear buyers described as fitness-engaged are the stated audience for bars eaten 'for workouts or on-the-go snacking', and the largest reach among the fitness-adjacent publishers here.
recommended.risk: Apparel shoppers are in a fashion mindset; crossover to a consumable food purchase at checkout may be weaker than the fitness framing suggests.

recommended.name: Pop & Sip
recommended.tier_reason: The score only saw a partial wellness tag overlap; the notes describe exactly this brand's positioning — 'Health-curious but indulgence-seeking' is precisely who buys a protein bar chosen for taste, and the shared playful tone matches the cardboard line.
recommended.rationale: Someone buying a better-for-you soda is already paying for a healthier version of something that still has to taste good, which is the whole pitch; $35 against a $42 basket is an easy add.
recommended.risk: Only 5.2M monthly impressions, so it can carry limited budget and results will read slowly.

test.name: Swiftcart
test.tier_reason: Excluded on weak fit, but the record matches the brand's stated occasions directly: 'Impulse-friendly' high-frequency convenience buyers at a $28 basket, with 84M impressions to read a taste-led snack offer quickly.
test.rationale: Convenience-delivery shoppers buying snacks on impulse are the on-the-go snacking half of the audience, and the $35 offer is close to their $28 typical basket; the open question is whether a multi-bar DTC box converts against instant delivery.

evidence.quote: High-frequency purchasers. Late-night traffic spike. Impulse-friendly

test.risk: Late-night convenience/alcohol baskets skew indulgent rather than fitness, and the platform itself likely sells bars for same-day delivery, undercutting a shipped box.

test.name: Pantrygood
test.tier_reason: Scored as weak fit on missing shared values, but this is a natural/organic pantry replenishment basket — snacks belong in it, and the $86 average order makes a $35 bar box a trivial add.
test.rationale: Pantry-stocking subscribers buy shelf-stable snacks on a replenishment cycle, which matches the brand's replenishment occasion; worth testing whether a taste-led pitch lands with shoppers the notes call 'Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims'.

evidence.quote: Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

test.risk: An organic grocer likely already stocks competing bars, and its values-driven shoppers want ingredient claims this brand doesn't make.

test.name: Daily Form
test.rationale: Supplement subscribers replenish nutrition products on a cycle, so a bar fits the basket, but the notes flag an audience 'skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims' and this brand's entire pitch is taste rather than science.

evidence.quote: Audience skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims

test.risk: A 'tastes good, not like cardboard' pitch may read as unserious to a science-forward, 89% female supplement audience; reach is also small at 4.2M.

test.name: Cloudfoot
test.tier_reason: Excluded as weak fit, but this publisher sells activewear and performance footwear, so the purchase moment is a fitness one; the gender-balanced 25-45 audience also matches the assumed 25-45 buyer better than the female-heavy wellness publishers.
test.rationale: Buying running shoes or activewear signals active use, making workout fuel a plausible next purchase; the uncertainty is whether 'Tech-adjacent urban professionals' bought for comfort and commuting rather than training.

evidence.quote: Tech-adjacent urban professionals. Comfort + sustainability messaging

test.risk: A $118 comfort-shoe basket may be a style purchase, not a fitness one, and 5.8M impressions limits how fast this reads.

test_plan.risk: A $118 comfort-shoe basket may be a style purchase, not a fitness one, and 5.8M impressions limits how fast this reads.
test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $10.50 target after 14 days: move it to core.

frequency_cap.rationale: Offers appear once, right after checkout; repeating them reads as spam.

experiment.graduate_rule: After 14 days, move a test publisher to core if its CPA is at or below target; cut any placement above max CPA.
experiment.notes: Creatives rotate evenly until each has enough conversions to compare.

assumptions: Assumed a mid price tier and about a $35 first order, since no pricing was given.
Assumed one-time purchases rather than a subscription.
Assumed a broad adult audience with no gender skew.
Allowable CPA is 30% of first order value (one time); replace with real margin and LTV.
warnings: The review questions whether this is a B2B or consumer business: offering_type_doubt
Target CPA is based on an assumed order value. Confirm price before launch.

launch_summary.summary: $8,500 of the $10,000 budget goes to three core publishers — Studiogrid, Movewell and Pop & Sip — where the checkout itself is a fitness or better-for-you-food moment. The remaining $1,500 spreads across four tests (Swiftcart, Pantrygood, Daily Form, Cloudfoot) to learn whether replenishment and impulse snacking baskets convert, with each promoted or cut after 14 days against the $10.50 target. Ads run five personas, from the Fitness Enthusiast to the Busy Parent, with the Gen Z Aesthete creative used only on Pop & Sip, Swiftcart and Daily Form.
uncertainties: The $35 first order value is assumed, and the $10.50 target cost per new customer is 30% of it, so a wrong price moves every bid.
The review flags doubt about whether this is a consumer or B2B business, which would change the whole publisher list.
One-time purchase is assumed rather than subscription; if shoppers reorder, the payback rule is too strict.
Daily Form's science-forward, 89% female supplement audience may read a taste-led pitch as unserious, and Cloudfoot's $118 comfort-shoe basket may not be a fitness purchase at all.
questions: What is your actual average first order value and margin?
Do customers buy once, or is there a subscription or repeat cycle we should price against?
Is this purely direct-to-consumer, or is there a wholesale or business side?
